A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RNN short-term memory study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures and appendices are readable, allowing reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original toy-model simulations and experiments with over 35,000 RNNs, including mechanism distributions, scaling fits and a no-delay control.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments with approximately 80,000 RNNs, including revised scaling analyses, mechanism diagnostics and additional control experiments.

M1.justification: The RNN architectures and ghost/limit-cycle toy models are retained. However, the auxiliary mechanism-classification procedure changes from firing-rate dispersion (OM, v1 S2.2) to a spectral-power ratio computed from correlations of principal components (MDI, v2 S3.4.1). This revises an analysis component without replacing the central models.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate delayed activation, delayed cue discrimination with and without post-reaction periods, and a no-delay cue-response control. v2's larger time constant and expanded parameter sweeps concern model configurations within these retained tasks, rather than new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates additional external baseline methods. Slow-point and limit-cycle mechanisms remain the principal comparisons; LSTMs, GRUs, Transformers and newly discussed alternative approaches are cited rather than experimentally benchmarked.

E3.justification: The empirical evaluation pipeline changes substantially. v2 normalizes reaction reliability by total output, revises success/failure criteria and training-window definitions, and replaces modified-ReLU cutoff estimation with exponential-saturation or sigmoid fits (v1 S2 versus v2 S3.4). It also extends the plotted rank-2 delay sweep and adds experiments with tau = 20 ms.

E4.justification: v2 adds a time-constant robustness study (Fig. S5), mechanism-discrimination diagnostics and a direct empirical test of slow-point scaling (Fig. S3), and representative successful and failed trajectories (Fig. S4). The existing no-delay ablation gains a quantitative scaling analysis in Fig. S6; it is not a newly introduced task.

E5.justification: Rank-2 repetitions increase from 10 to 100 networks per condition (v1 Fig. 4C; v2 Fig. 3C). v2 also tabulates seed counts and newly specifies covariance-based Monte Carlo estimation of 95% confidence intervals. v1 already reports regression uncertainties and Fisher tests with Bonferroni correction, so statistical reporting is expanded rather than introduced.

E6.justification: Without/with post-reaction periods, v1 Fig. 6 reports slopes of -2.40 ± 0.36 and -1.57 ± 0.18; v2 Fig. 4 reports decay-exponent magnitudes of 2.72 ± 0.07 and 2.65 ± 0.23. v2 additionally reports slow-point scaling of 4.05 ± 0.10 and no-delay scaling of 0.38 ± 0.02. These are revised or added results under changed analyses and expanded experiments, not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The central ghost and limit-cycle derivations and scaling exponents are retained, moving from v1 S1 to v2 S2. Limited mathematical changes include the revised reliability definition and replacement of OM with the formally defined MDI (v2 Eqs. S37–S38); no new central scaling theorem or proof appears.

C1.justification: The two-mechanism, task-design and critical-learning-rate contributions remain. v2's introduction strengthens the empirical contribution from extracting scaling laws to explicitly claiming quantitative agreement with theoretical predictions within error bars. This refines the central validation claim without changing the research objective.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly cautions that the toy mechanisms are non-exhaustive and discusses transient, high-dimensional alternatives, refining v1's approximate-bound framing. It also drops v1's interpretation that adding a post-reaction period yields more efficient scaling, instead emphasizing agreement with theoretical ranges and changes in mechanism selection.

D1.justification: v2 adds extensive implementation and reproduction information: Euler updates, weighted MSE, optimizer settings, initialization, training schedules, parameter grids, hardware and figure-specific configurations (S3–S4). It states that code and model data are available through GitHub and Zenodo, replacing v1's release promise. Newly disclosed training details do not establish that previously unspecified settings changed.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted literature on activity-silent and synaptic memory, reservoir/transient dynamics, universal approximation and low-dimensional computation. These additions broaden context and qualify applicability while retaining the principal connections to earlier ghost-model, low-rank RNN and sequential-memory research.

P1.justification: The introduction and discussion are extensively rewritten around three explicit research questions, with machine-learning motivation moved forward from the discussion. The separate conclusion is absorbed into concluding remarks, results gain explanatory subheadings, and the appendix is reorganized into background, theory, experimental methods and reproduction sections.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout and substantially restructures the figures. Fig. 1 combines revised mechanism diagrams with task illustrations; Fig. 2 contracts from five cases to three; v1 Fig. 3 moves to Fig. S1; theoretical and empirical phase diagrams are consolidated into Fig. 4. New diagnostic/control panels and Table S1 further expand the presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the connection between theory and evidence through direct slow-point scaling tests, mechanism diagnostics and a time-constant control. Its expanded methods and stated code/data access also address important reproducibility gaps in v1. Some inconsistent figure references and parameter descriptions in S4 limit reproducibility, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and documentation.
